Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles)
soo-KOHT
noun (proper, biblical feast)
From Hebrew sukkoth, booths or temporary shelters; the autumn feast also called the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths.

Biblical Definition

Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths, is the autumn festival the LORD appointed in Leviticus 23:34-43, when Israel dwelt seven days in booths in remembrance that the LORD made them dwell in booths when He brought them out of Egypt. It was a feast of harvest joy and of holy memory: the people gathered the fruit of the land, took the boughs of goodly trees and willows of the brook, and rejoiced before the LORD their God, while their frail leafy shelters preached that their fathers had been pilgrims sustained by God through the wilderness. Yet like all the appointed feasts, Sukkot was a shadow of good things to come, and its substance is Christ. The booth in which Israel dwelt foretold the great mystery that God Himself would tabernacle among men, for the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us—literally, tabernacled among us—and we beheld His glory. The transient shelter pointed to the incarnate Son who pitched His tent in our nature to bring His pilgrim people home. Moreover, on the last day, that great day of the feast of Tabernacles, Jesus stood and cried, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink—offering Himself as the living water the feast's water-pouring had only signified. Thus Sukkot finds its fulfillment in Christ, who is God dwelling with men, the harvest joy of His redeemed, and the spring of living water for all who thirst. The shadow has passed; the believer keeps the feast in the substance, rejoicing in the God who has tabernacled with us and will at last dwell with His people forever.

Webster 1828 Definition

Sukkot is Israel's Feast of Tabernacles, dwelling in booths in remembrance of the wilderness, fulfilled in Christ who tabernacled among men.

SUKKOT, noun. From Hebrew sukkoth, booths or temporary shelters.

The autumn feast in which Israel dwelt seven days in booths, also called the Feast of Tabernacles.

A feast of harvest joy and remembrance of the LORD's care in the wilderness.

A type fulfilled in Christ, who tabernacled among men and gives living water.

Scripture appoints it: "The fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the feast of tabernacles for seven days unto the LORD" (Leviticus 23:34).

Key Scripture

Lev 23:34 — "Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, The fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the feast of tabernacles for seven days unto the LORD."

Lev 23:43 — "That your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God."

Joh 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Joh 7:37 — "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink."

Modern Corruption

Sukkot's typology is rightly read as shadow fulfilled in Christ, against any view that empties it of Him.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger is not a culture-war grievance but a failure of biblical reading—treating the feast either as a relic of mere ritual law with no abiding meaning, or as a ceremony Christians must still keep in its Mosaic form, as though the shadow had not yielded to the substance. Both miss the point. The feast was appointed by the LORD as a true shadow whose body is Christ, and to read it rightly is to see Him in it.

The principle to recover is the typological unity of Scripture under one covenant of grace. Israel's booths preached the pilgrim life sustained by God and foretold the day when God would tabernacle with men; the Word made flesh dwelt—tabernacled—among us, and on the great day of the feast offered Himself as the living water it signified. The believer therefore does not return to the Mosaic shadows, nor does he despise them; he beholds Christ in them, keeps the feast in its substance, and waits for the consummation when God shall dwell with His people and be their God forever.

Hebrew Roots

The feast rests on the LORD's appointment in Leviticus 23 and finds its fulfillment in the incarnate Christ.

expand to see more

Leviticus 23:34 appoints the seven-day feast of tabernacles in the seventh month.

Leviticus 23:42-43 commands Israel to dwell in booths in remembrance of the wilderness.

John 1:14 declares the Word made flesh dwelt—tabernacled—among us.

John 7:37-38 shows Christ offering living water on the great day of the feast.

The feast is a shadow whose substance and fulfillment is Christ Himself.

Usage

"Used of the appointed feast: "Israel kept Sukkot in the seventh month.""

"Used of the booths: "they dwelt in Sukkot booths for seven days.""

"Used typologically: "Sukkot foreshadowed God tabernacling with men in Christ.""
